prompt: According to this lesson, what is the commonest failure in handling an incident?

choices.text: Slow repair of the bug
choices.why: Repair speed matters less than having someone in charge early.

choices.text: Too many alarms firing at once
choices.why: That is a separate problem, lesson 14's.

choices.text: Slow declaration
choices.why: Right. Forty minutes of private investigation with nobody in charge, each assuming someone else is talking to customers.

choices.text: Writing the postmortem too late
choices.why: The review comes after; the failure named here comes first.

prompt: Unsure whether an incident is SEV1 or SEV2, what should the person declaring it do?
hint: Compare the cost of each mistake.

choices.text: Declare SEV1
choices.why: Right. Downgrading later costs one message.

choices.text: Declare SEV2 and wait for more data
choices.why: Under-declaring costs the hour in which nobody was in charge.

choices.text: Ask the team to vote in the channel
choices.why: A vote is the meeting a severity scale exists to avoid.

choices.text: Not declare until the cause is known
choices.why: The cause often comes last; declaring is about impact.

prompt: A customer reported the outage before any alert fired. What does the review do with that fact?
hint: Detection is one of the review's questions.

choices.text: Nothing, since the outage was fixed
choices.why: The next one will be found the same way.

choices.text: Records a gap in alerting, to close
choices.why: Right. Every customer-first detection is a gap in the alerting.

choices.text: Thanks the customer and closes it
choices.why: Polite, and the alerting gap stays open.

choices.text: Lowers the severity, since customers knew
choices.why: Customer awareness makes it worse, not smaller.

prompt: Match each incident role to its job.

pairs.right: Decides, assigns and keeps the clock

prompt: Which role should never be held by the same person as the operations lead?
hint: Attention on the system or on the whole.

choices.text: Scribe
choices.why: Combining these is not ideal, but command is the one never shared.

choices.text: Communications lead
choices.why: Possible in a small team; command is the one to keep apart.

choices.text: Customer
choices.why: Customers hold no incident role.

choices.text: Incident commander
choices.why: Right. The person fixing the system cannot also coordinate everybody.

prompt: Which status update follows this lesson's rules?
hint: Observed, since when, not affected, next update.

choices.text: We broke checkout with a bad deploy by the payments team; it will be fixed within ten minutes, sorry.
choices.why: It blames a team, guesses the cause and promises a time nobody can.

choices.text: Some customers see errors paying since 14:02; placed orders are fine; next update 14:45.
choices.why: Right. Observed, since when, what is not affected, and the next update.

choices.text: Everything is fine.
choices.why: It contradicts what customers see, which costs more trust than silence.

choices.text: Investigating a database problem.
choices.why: It names a cause nobody has confirmed, and no next update.

prompt: Checkout is failing after a deploy, and the cause is not yet understood. What does the commander ask for first?

choices.text: The rollback, restoring service before anything else
choices.why: Right. Restore service first; understand it with the graph green.

choices.text: A full analysis before touching anything
choices.why: Customers keep failing during the analysis.

choices.text: A list of everyone who approved the deploy
choices.why: Blame does not stop the bleeding, and the review is blameless.

choices.text: A new deploy with a fix written now
choices.why: A rushed fix of an un-understood cause is a second gamble.

prompt: In the lab's timeline, which event came last?

choices.text: The deployment
choices.why: It came first, at 16:58:53.

choices.text: The first 503 on /checkout
choices.why: It came eight seconds after the deployment.

choices.text: The alarm going into ALARM
choices.why: Right. The change, then the symptom, then the alarm.

choices.text: The 503 on /cart
choices.why: The alarm came ten seconds after it.

prompt: Why build the timeline from the systems' own records rather than from the team's memory?
hint: The gaps that matter are short.

choices.text: People lie in reviews
choices.why: The review is blameless so that they do not need to.

choices.text: Records are required by AWS
choices.why: No such requirement; they are simply more accurate.

choices.text: It is faster to read than to ask
choices.why: Maybe, but accuracy is the reason.

choices.text: Memory fails in the short gaps
choices.why: Right. Seconds between a change and its first symptom are invisible to memory.

prompt: To merge times from different tools without confusion, every source in a timeline should use one time zone, usually ___.

hint: What do people do when they expect blame?

choices.text: Fear of blame hides the details
choices.why: Right. And the system that allowed it stays there for the next person.

choices.text: To be polite to whoever made the mistake
choices.why: Politeness is not the reason; information is.

choices.text: Because nobody ever makes mistakes in operations
choices.why: People always make mistakes; the system decides what they cost.

choices.text: Because the law forbids naming people
choices.why: It is a practice for learning, not a legal rule.

prompt: Which of these is an action that changes the system?
hint: Somebody can do it and finish it.

choices.text: Everyone will be more careful when deploying
choices.why: Nobody can be assigned it, and nobody can tell when it is done.

choices.text: Remind the team in the next meeting
choices.why: A reminder fades; nothing persists.

choices.text: Find out who approved it
choices.why: That is blame, and it changes nothing.

choices.text: A canary with a narrow alarm
choices.why: Right. A canary alarmed on the new version only is a change somebody makes, reviews and finishes.

prompt: Put the questions of a postmortem in the order this lesson asks them.
hint: From what happened to what changes.
trap: Actions before the factors is the slip: the actions answer the factors.

prompt: Which belong in the first five minutes of a SEV1? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Declare it in the agreed channel
choices.why: Yes. One place for everything about it.

choices.text: Name the incident commander
choices.why: Yes. Somebody decides from now on.

choices.text: Find the root cause
choices.why: No. Mitigation first; the cause can wait for the green graph.

choices.text: Write the postmortem
choices.why: No. That comes days later.

choices.text: Plan the first customer update
choices.why: Yes. Within fifteen minutes for a SEV1.

prompt: Impact began at 14:02, the alert fired at 14:09 and service was restored at 14:31. What was the time to mitigate, in minutes?
hint: From the start of impact to restoration.
